text: Every resource you've built so far in this path — the Terraform infrastructure, the Kubernetes workloads, the monitoring stack — costs real money every hour it runs, whether or not anyone's watching the bill. FinOps, short for cloud financial operations, is the discipline built around that fact. The FinOps Foundation maintains the industry's reference framework for it, organized into three phases that repeat as a continuous loop: Inform, Optimize, and Operate. Learn this vocabulary by name — it shows up in job postings and inside Azure and AWS's own cost tools.

Inform comes first, because nothing downstream works without it. This phase is about building real-time visibility into current and forecasted spend, and allocating that cost to the team or project that actually generated it — which only works if resources are tagged consistently, a topic Lesson 19 covers in depth. Optimize is the phase most people picture when they hear cost optimization: finding idle or oversized resources, right-sizing against actual observed usage, and evaluating commitment discounts like Reserved Instances or Savings Plans. But Optimize can't succeed on untrustworthy data — it depends entirely on Inform having already produced accurate, attributed numbers.

That dependency is the whole point of drawing this as a loop instead of a one-time project. A team can't optimize spend it can't see, and it can't hold anyone accountable for spend it can't attribute to a real owner. Inform has to keep running continuously, not just at the start of a cost-cutting initiative, because cloud footprints change every day as new resources get provisioned and old ones get forgotten.

Operate is where FinOps becomes an ongoing business process rather than a cleanup sprint: setting goals and KPIs for cloud spend, defining who owns what, and continuously improving the other two phases as the organization grows. And none of this runs on one team alone. Finance owns budgets and forecasting. Engineering holds the only hands that can actually right-size or shut down a resource. Business and product supply the context that tells you whether a spend increase is waste or just the cost of real growth — skip any one of those three, and FinOps tends to collapse into an adversarial cost-police-versus-engineers fight.

That's the framework: Inform for visibility and attribution, Optimize for acting on it, Operate for turning it into a lasting process, with the three personas — Finance, Engineering, and Business — sharing ownership of the loop. Next lesson, you'll see Inform in action for real, reading an actual Azure Cost Analysis view and an AWS Cost Explorer report, grouping spend by service, by tag, and by account.
